passage: When Ms Iyer called Varun to read aloud from the English reader, he stood with the book close to his face and started blinking fast, again and again. From the next bench Nitin whispered, “He didn't even look at it last night, see how his eyes are going.” Ms Iyer heard. “Blinking doesn't tell us that, Nitin. Many people blink more when they're nervous or tired.” She turned back. “Take your time, Varun.” Varun took a breath, put a finger under the line and read on more slowly. By the third sentence the blinking had eased.

qa.q: Who whispered about Varun's eyes?
qa.a: Nitin whispered about them.

qa.q: What might Varun have been feeling while he blinked, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Most likely nervous about reading in front of the class, since it eased once he slowed down and put a finger under the line. Tiredness can also make people blink more.

qa.q: What did Ms Iyer do that helped?
qa.a: She told the class that blinking does not show what Nitin claimed, and she gave Varun time, which let him settle. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nitin see it after Ms Iyer's words?
qa.a: He may realise he jumped to a conclusion from a cue with many causes, and perhaps feel a little embarrassed.

grounding: A child blinks a lot when nervous reading aloud, which a classmate reads as not having prepared.

passage:
“Read your poem for me, Vishal.”
“Okay.” Vishal held the notebook and blinked, blink, blink, blink.
“Why are you blinking so much?” said Usha. “Did you copy it?”
“No! I wrote it.”
“Your eyes are going like a butterfly.”
Vishal rubbed them. “I'm nervous. And they're tired from the screen lesson.”
Usha put the notebook down. “I'm sorry. I shouldn't decide from your eyes. Read slowly, I'm listening.”
He read. The poem was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Vishal's poem about?
qa.a: It was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Vishal probably feeling when he said “No! I wrote it”?
qa.a: Hurt and nervous about being doubted, since he right away explained the blinking as nerves and tired eyes. He may also have felt worried his poem would not be liked.

qa.q: What did Usha do that repaired the moment?
qa.a: She apologised, stopped judging by his eyes and listened, which let him read without extra pressure.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had kept believing he copied?
qa.a: Vishal might feel distrusted and be even more nervous next time, and the poem would go unheard.

grounding: A child blinks from nerves and tiredness; blinking is not evidence of dishonesty.

passage:
Monday: Tejas saw Hrithik narrow his eyes at him across the classroom. He's angry about the cricket match, Tejas thought, and stayed away from him all break.
Wednesday: Hrithik narrowed his eyes again, first at Tejas, then at the board. Tejas noticed the sun glaring on the board through the window. “Are you okay?” he whispered. “I can't read with that glare,” said Hrithik.
Friday: Sir moved Hrithik's seat, and Tejas saved him a place at cricket.

qa.q: Where was the sun glaring on Wednesday?
qa.a: The sun was glaring on the board through the window.

qa.q: What did Tejas think on Monday when Hrithik narrowed his eyes, and how reliable was that reading?
qa.a: He thought Hrithik was angry about the cricket match. It was only a guess, as Wednesday showed that the narrowing could come from glare.

qa.q: What could Tejas do differently from Monday?
qa.a: Check the context first, such as the light and whether Hrithik can see, or ask kindly, as he did on Wednesday.

qa.q: How might Hrithik have felt when Tejas stayed away on Monday?
qa.a: Confused or left out, since he probably did not know why Tejas was avoiding him.

grounding: A child reads a classmate's narrowed eyes as anger, but it was squinting at glare.

passage:
“Listen, Arohi,” said Kamal Mama, “when I was your age, my friend Sunil squinted hard at me during a cricket match. I decided he was cross about a catch I dropped. I stayed away from him for a week. Then I saw him squinting at the scoreboard, at the road signs, at everything far away. He needed spectacles, that's all! Nothing to do with me.” He shook his head. “Now I look at the light and whether the person can see before I decide anything. Or I ask.”
“And Sunil?”
“He was hurt I'd gone quiet.”

qa.q: How long did Kamal Mama stay away from Sunil?
qa.a: He stayed away for a week.

qa.q: What did Kamal Mama first think Sunil's squint meant, and what did he later realise?
qa.a: He first thought Sunil was cross about a dropped catch. Later he saw Sunil squinting at everything far away and realised it was about seeing.

qa.q: What would you advise Arohi to do when someone squints at her?
qa.a: Look at the light and whether the person can see well, and ask kindly before deciding they are angry.

qa.q: How might Sunil have felt when Kamal went quiet?
qa.a: Confused and hurt, since Kamal says he was hurt that Kamal had gone quiet. He had probably done nothing wrong.

grounding: A child misreads a squint as anger; checking the context avoids unfair conclusions.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Last week Shreya Ma'am told me off in front of everyone for talking. I looked at the floor and my cheeks felt hot. “Look at me when I'm speaking to you,” she said, and I couldn't. I wasn't being rude. I felt small and my eyes just ran away. At home my Ajji says looking down shows respect for elders, so I don't know what it looked like to Ma'am. After class she said, “I think you were embarrassed. Next time I'll talk to you quietly.” I felt a lot better.

qa.q: Who told Manjula off in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shreya Ma'am told her off in front of everyone.

qa.q: Why couldn't Manjula look at Shreya Ma'am, and what else might lowered eyes mean?
qa.a: She felt small and embarrassed, so her eyes ran away. Lowered eyes can also show respect, as her Ajji says.

qa.q: What did Shreya Ma'am do next that helped?
qa.a: She named that Manjula was probably embarrassed and promised to talk to her quietly next time.

qa.q: How might Shreya Ma'am have read Manjula's lowered eyes at first?
qa.a: As rudeness or defiance, since she asked Manjula to look at her. After class she read it as embarrassment instead.

grounding: A child looks away when scolded in public, from shame or shyness, not defiance.

subtype: Averting gaze when embarrassed or corrected [Expressing]
passage: Note from Afreen, Class 4 teacher. Jagdish looked at his shoes and rubbed his ear when I praised his drawing in assembly. Earlier, when I corrected his spelling, he also looked away. His grandfather, who collects him, says looking down is how Jagdish shows respect to elders at home. So this may be respect, or embarrassment at attention, or both. I can't be sure which. Next steps: I will praise Jagdish privately, I won't ask for eye contact, and I will check in with him with a quiet question at the end of the day.

qa.q: Where did Afreen praise Jagdish's drawing?
qa.a: She praised it in assembly.

qa.q: What might Jagdish have felt when he looked at his shoes after the praise, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Likely embarrassment or shyness about public attention. It could also be respect, as his grandfather says looking down is how he shows respect to elders.

qa.q: What did Afreen decide to do next?
qa.a: To praise Jagdish privately, to stop asking for eye contact and to check in with a quiet question at the end of the day.

qa.q: How might Jagdish's grandfather see the lowered eyes?
qa.a: As a sign of respect, since he says that is how Jagdish greets elders at home.

grounding: A child looks away when praised or corrected, from shyness or shame, and in some families as respect.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage:
“Sonali, why do you look down when Nanaji talks to you?” asked Saurabh, who had just moved to Delhi from Manchester.
“It's respect. Looking straight at elders can seem rude.”
“At my old school, looking down would mean you were hiding something.”
“That's silly! I'm not hiding anything.”
“I know, I know. I just think it's different.”
Nanaji laughed from his chair. “Both my grandchildren are honest, whichever way they look.”
Sonali looked up at him and smiled. Saurabh grinned.

qa.q: Where had Saurabh just moved from?
qa.a: He had just moved to Delhi from Manchester.

qa.q: What might Sonali have felt when Saurabh said looking down would mean hiding something?
qa.a: A bit offended and defensive, since she called it silly, though she then listened when he said it is just different. She may also have wondered how others read her.

qa.q: How could the cousins avoid misunderstanding each other?
qa.a: By asking what each way of looking means to the other, and remembering that neither lowered eyes nor steady eye contact proves honesty or disrespect.

qa.q: How does Nanaji see the two children's eyes?
qa.a: He judges them as honest whichever way they look, so he does not treat the eyes as proof.

grounding: Lowered eyes with elders can show respect while steady eye contact can signal honesty elsewhere; neither is proof.

subtype: Eye contact norms with elders in India [Mismatch]
passage: In my old school in Pune, I looked down when teachers spoke, to show respect. Now in Toronto, Mr Vikas said, “Please look at me so I know you're listening.” I tried, and my eyes felt hot and strange. At recess I told him that where I come from, looking down is polite. He said, “Thanks for telling me. I didn't know. I'll remember that you're listening even when you look down.” Now I look up sometimes and sometimes I don't, and it is fine either way.

qa.q: Which city did Sunaina move to?
qa.a: She moved to Toronto.

qa.q: How did Sunaina feel when Mr Vikas asked her to look at him, and what else might explain his request?
qa.a: Uncomfortable, since her eyes felt hot and strange. Mr Vikas probably wanted a sign she was listening, not to be unkind.

qa.q: What worked well in how Sunaina handled it?
qa.a: She told him calmly what lowered eyes mean where she comes from, and that gave him what he needed to understand her.

qa.q: How might Mr Vikas have first read Sunaina's lowered eyes?
qa.a: Perhaps as not listening or being shy. He asked for eye contact to check, and later changed when she explained.

grounding: Eye contact norms differ between families and schools; neither shows honesty or disrespect.

passage: I'm Bhupen, and I saw my sister Sabina roll her eyes when Ma asked her to fold the clothes. Ma's face went tight. “What was that?” “Nothing.” I couldn't tell if Sabina was bored, tired from school, or still angry about the argument earlier. Ma took a breath. “Sabina, you seem fed up. What's up?” Sabina sat down on the bed. “I've folded the clothes three times this week and Bhupen never does.” Ma nodded. “Fair. Bhupen, you do it tomorrow.” I sulked, but it was fair.

qa.q: What did Ma ask Sabina to fold?
qa.a: She asked her to fold the clothes.

qa.q: What was Sabina probably feeling behind the eye-roll, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: Fed up, because she felt the chore was unfair, as she said she had folded the clothes three times and Bhupen never does. It could also have been tiredness or boredom, as Bhupen guessed.

qa.q: How did Ma's question open a better talk?
qa.a: She named that Sabina seemed fed up and asked what was up, instead of arguing about the eye-roll. That let the real complaint come out.

qa.q: How does Bhupen feel about the outcome?
qa.a: He sulked, but he admits it was fair, so he seems to feel a bit caught out and also accepts it. 😅

grounding: An eye-roll signals annoyance and a calm question opens a better talk.

passage:
Monday: when Ms Anjali reminded the class about the spelling test, Elizabeth rolled her eyes. Ms Anjali said nothing but noticed.
Wednesday: Elizabeth rolled her eyes again. After class Ms Anjali said calmly, “I noticed the eye-roll. What's going on?” Elizabeth shrugged. “The words are too easy. I finish first and wait.” Ms Anjali nodded. “Thank you for telling me.”
Friday: Ms Anjali handed Elizabeth an extra list of long words. There was no eye-roll. Elizabeth said, “Can I have the hardest one first?”

qa.q: On which day did Ms Anjali ask Elizabeth what was going on?
qa.a: She asked on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Elizabeth probably feeling when she rolled her eyes on Monday, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably bored, since she later said the words were too easy and she finishes first and waits. It could also have been mild annoyance at being reminded.

qa.q: How did Ms Anjali's approach work better than scolding?
qa.a: She calmly asked what was going on, so Elizabeth explained, and the answer led to an extra list that solved the boredom.

qa.q: How might Ms Anjali have felt when she first saw the eye-roll?
qa.a: Possibly a little stung or puzzled, but she said nothing and waited to ask privately. That gave her a real answer instead of an argument.

grounding: An eye-roll signals boredom or annoyance; calmly asking what is wrong opens a better conversation.

passage:
“Why are you making that face?” said Tenzin. “You look like a fish.”
“I'm not.”
“You're sucking your cheeks in. Are you angry with me?”
Nirmala let her cheeks go. “No. I'm nervous about my dance recital tomorrow. I bite the inside of my cheek when I'm nervous. Don't stare.”
“Sorry.” Tenzin scratched his head. “Want to practise in front of me? I'll just watch. No comments on faces.”
Nirmala took a breath. “Okay. Just the first part.”

qa.q: What is Nirmala nervous about?
qa.a: She is nervous about her dance recital tomorrow.

qa.q: What was Nirmala feeling when she drew in her cheeks, and what did Tenzin first think it meant?
qa.a: She was nervous about the recital, and the cheek habit calms her. Tenzin first thought she was angry with him, since it looked like a grimace.

qa.q: What could Tenzin do to support Nirmala?
qa.a: Do what he offered: watch quietly, skip comments about her face and let her practise at her own pace.

qa.q: Why might Tenzin have misread Nirmala's face?
qa.a: Drawn-in cheeks look like a grimace or a scowl, and he could not see her worry. He asked instead of assuming, which helped.

grounding: Drawn-in cheeks and cheek biting are self-soothing from nerves, not ill will.

passage: I bite the inside of my cheek when I concentrate or get nervous. In class today Sunaina looked at me and asked, “Are you cross with someone?” I said, “No, I'm thinking.” Then I realised my face looks like a grimace when I do it. So I told her, “It's just a habit when I'm nervous about the test.” She said, “Oh, I do something too. I twist my hair.” We both laughed. I didn't feel so odd after that.

qa.q: What does Nandini do when she concentrates or gets nervous?
qa.a: She bites the inside of her cheek.

qa.q: What was Nandini feeling when Sunaina asked if she was cross, and what did Sunaina think?
qa.a: Nandini was nervous about the test and concentrating. Sunaina thought Nandini looked cross, because the cheek biting looks like a grimace.

qa.q: What worked when Nandini explained her habit?
qa.a: She said plainly that it is a habit when nervous, so Sunaina understood and shared her own habit of twisting her hair.

qa.q: How might Sunaina have felt when Nandini said she was only thinking?
qa.a: Probably relieved that Nandini was not upset with someone. She was also comfortable enough to admit her own habit.

grounding: Cheek biting from nerves looks like a grimace but is self-soothing.

passage: At lunch today Minakshi wrinkled her nose when I opened my tiffin. It was methi paratha. My cheeks went hot and I shut the lid. I thought, she thinks my food is yucky. I stopped eating. Minakshi noticed and asked, “Did I do something?” I said, “You made a face at my lunch.” She looked around and laughed. “No! Someone at the next bench opened a boiled egg and it smells so strong!” I hadn't even noticed. She said, “Your paratha smells lovely, can I try a bit?”

qa.q: What was in Sharmila's tiffin?
qa.a: Her tiffin had methi paratha.

qa.q: How did Sharmila feel when Minakshi wrinkled her nose, and what did she think it meant?
qa.a: She felt hurt and embarrassed, since her cheeks went hot and she shut the lid, thinking Minakshi found her food yucky. She had not noticed the smell from the next bench.

qa.q: How did Minakshi's question help?
qa.a: She asked, “Did I do something?” which let Sharmila say what she saw and let Minakshi explain the real reason.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when she learned Sharmila thought it was about the paratha?
qa.a: Probably surprised and a bit sorry that her face had caused hurt. Her offer to try a bit shows she wanted to make it right.

grounding: A child sees a friend wrinkle her nose at lunch and feels hurt, but asking shows it was another smell.

passage: Note from Bidisha, class teacher. At lunch, Lakshmi's friend wrinkled her nose while Lakshmi was unpacking her tiffin. Lakshmi shut the box and stopped eating. I sat beside her and asked quietly what was wrong. She said, “She thinks my food smells.” I asked the friend, gently, what the face was about. She said the bin near their bench smelled sour. Lakshmi opened the box again. I suggested to them that when a face worries you, you can ask, “Was that about my food?” They tried the sentence together.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do after her friend wrinkled her nose?
qa.a: She shut the box and stopped eating.

qa.q: What was Lakshmi probably feeling when she shut her tiffin, and what else could the friend's face have meant?
qa.a: Probably hurt and self-conscious, thinking her food was being rejected. The friend's face was actually about the sour smell from the bin.

qa.q: What small step did Bidisha suggest for next time?
qa.a: That when a face worries them, they ask something like “Was that about my food?” instead of assuming, and she had them practise it together.

qa.q: How might the friend have felt on learning Lakshmi had been hurt?
qa.a: Probably surprised and sorry, since she did not mean anything by it. She joined in practising the question, which suggests she wanted to make it right.

grounding: A child feels hurt by a wrinkled nose at her lunch; asking kindly avoids assuming rejection.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage: In the school hall the quiz scores went up on the board. Mahima's team was one point behind Deepak's. Deepak's upper lip lifted on one side as he glanced across at her. Mahima's lower lip began to tremble; she pressed it flat and stared at her knees. Mr Dutta, the teacher, saw both. “Five-minute break, everyone. Water at the back.” He walked over and said quietly, “Want to step out with me for a moment?” Later he asked Deepak privately what had happened before the round. Deepak shrugged. “She said in the corridor that we'd never win.”

qa.q: How far behind was Mahima's team?
qa.a: Mahima's team was one point behind.

qa.q: What might Mahima's trembling lip suggest she was feeling, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Most likely she was holding back tears and felt embarrassed in front of classmates, since she pressed it flat and stared at her knees. It could also be nerves about the next round.

qa.q: How did Mr Dutta protect the children's dignity?
qa.a: He called a break for everyone and spoke quietly to Mahima, rather than pointing at either child in front of the hall.

qa.q: How might Deepak see his own curled lip?
qa.a: He may have meant scorn, given what he says was said in the corridor, but he might also not have known his face was doing it. Asking him privately let the earlier events come out.

grounding: A child curls a lip at a rival and another's lip trembles holding back tears; the adult protects dignity.

subtype: Curling a lip and lip trembling in embarrassment [Mismatch]
passage: I'm Pema, and I sit next to Ira in art class. When Ms Rao chose Dorji's painting for the corridor display, Ira's lip curled up on one side. Later, at her desk, the same lip trembled while she stared at her brush. I wasn't sure if she was jealous, or upset, or just tired, because she had stayed up finishing her painting. Ms Rao noticed too and asked, “Ira, could you help me pin the paintings? Yours has lovely colours too.” Ira nodded without speaking and followed her out.

qa.q: Whose painting did Ms Rao choose for the corridor display?
qa.a: She chose Dorji's painting.

qa.q: What might Ira have been feeling when her lip curled and later trembled, and what else could it be?
qa.a: Probably disappointment and some hurt pride at not being chosen. Pema could not be sure, and it might also have been tiredness or jealousy.

qa.q: How did Ms Rao handle the situation?
qa.a: She kept it private and gave Ira a job, and she said honestly that Ira's painting had lovely colours too, which protected her dignity.

qa.q: How might Pema feel watching Ira?
qa.a: Unsure and a bit worried for a friend, since she says she wasn't sure what the lip meant. She does not want to guess wrongly. 🤍

grounding: A child's curled lip and trembling lip after a rival is chosen; an observer cannot be sure and the adult protects dignity.

passage: When my mother, Kavitha, presses her lips into a thin line, I think she's angry. Last night she did it while reading a letter at the table, and I hid in my room for an hour, sure I'd done something. Finally I asked, “Are you angry with me?” She looked surprised. “No, Shalini. I'm just tired, and thinking about the guests coming.” I had worried for nothing. But once, when I broke a plate, the thin line was real. She said, “I was angry, and now I'm calm.” So I guess I'll always ask.

qa.q: What was Kavitha doing when she pressed her lips into a thin line last night?
qa.a: She was reading a letter at the table.

qa.q: What did Shalini think the tightened lips meant, and how did asking change her mind?
qa.a: She thought her mother was angry with her, so she hid in her room. When she asked, she learned her mother was just tired and thinking about the guests.

qa.q: What could Shalini do when she notices the thin line again?
qa.a: Ask a calm question, as she did last night, rather than hiding and guessing for an hour.

qa.q: How might Kavitha have felt when Shalini hid for an hour?
qa.a: Probably unaware at first, then surprised and perhaps a little sorry that her face worried her daughter. Her clear answer made things easier.

grounding: A child reads a parent's tightened lips as anger, sometimes right and sometimes wrong; a calm question helps.

passage: Note from Mahima, school counsellor. Sharmila told me she always knows when her father is angry because his lips go tight. Last week she was right: he had been shouted at by a customer at work. Yesterday she was wrong: he was just tired. She spent an evening avoiding him and felt worse. We practised one question she can ask calmly: “Are you upset with me, or just tired?” She said it aloud twice and laughed. I also told her that her father may not notice his face is doing it. She will try the question at home this week.

qa.q: What does Sharmila say her father's lips do when he is angry?
qa.a: She says his lips go tight.

qa.q: What was Sharmila probably feeling when she avoided her father yesterday, and why was she wrong?
qa.a: Probably worried he was angry with her, and it made her feel worse. She was wrong because he was just tired.

qa.q: What could Sharmila try at home this week?
qa.a: Ask the calm question they practised, “Are you upset with me, or just tired?”, instead of guessing from his lips.

qa.q: How might Sharmila's father feel if he learns she avoided him?
qa.a: He may be surprised and sorry that a tired face made her worry, and he may try to tell her when he is only tired.

grounding: A child reads a parent's tight lips as anger, sometimes correctly; a calm question helps.

passage: Rain was pouring and the school bus was due in six minutes. “Raincoat, Sarika,” said her mother, Irawati, holding it out. Sarika's chin jutted forward and she shook her head. Irawati's voice sharpened. “We have no time for this attitude.” Then she stopped, crouched and looked at her. “Tell me quickly. What's wrong?” Sarika's chin dropped a little. “The hood covers my eyes. Yesterday I couldn't see the road and a scooter splashed me.” Irawati took a breath. “Then take the umbrella.” Sarika nodded, and they ran for the gate just as the bus came.

qa.q: How many minutes until the school bus was due?
qa.a: It was due in six minutes.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when she jutted her chin, and what did Irawati first think it meant?
qa.a: She was worried about not being able to see the road under the hood. Irawati first read it as defiance, and Sarika's answer showed it was a wish to be heard.

qa.q: What worked in Irawati's change of approach?
qa.a: She stopped, crouched and asked, so Sarika could give her reason and they found a quick fix, the umbrella.

qa.q: How might Irawati feel when she heard Sarika's reason?
qa.a: Probably relieved and a bit sorry she had jumped to “attitude”. The time pressure made it easy to miss.

grounding: A child juts the jaw when refusing; listening first works better than a power struggle.

passage:
In the music room, Disha Ma'am asked Anand to sing the first verse alone. Anand's jaw shot forward. “No.”
Disha frowned, then sat down on a stool. “I see. You don't want to.”
“No.” His jaw stayed out.
“Can you tell me why?”
He looked at the floor. “Last time, some boys laughed at my voice.”
“Thank you for telling me.” Her voice was gentle. “What if you sing with the group and I stand next to you?”
His jaw relaxed. “Okay.”

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am ask Anand to sing?
qa.a: She asked him to sing the first verse alone.

qa.q: What was Anand feeling when his jaw shot forward, and what else could it have been?
qa.a: Probably afraid of being laughed at again, since he said some boys laughed at his voice last time. It could have looked like defiance to a teacher, but his jaw relaxed once he was heard.

qa.q: What did Disha Ma'am do that avoided a power struggle?
qa.a: She sat down, listened and asked why, then offered a smaller step of singing with the group beside him. 🙂

qa.q: How might Anand's classmates see his refusal?
qa.a: Some might think he was being stubborn, without knowing what happened last time. They may not realise he was afraid.

grounding: A child juts the jaw when refusing; listening first reveals fear and avoids a power struggle.
